It's possible, but would take a lot of extra work on your part. There are two main issues:

Issue A: Dependencies. When you compile something, it will need to also connect to other libraries on the computer. If you compile on one operating system, you may have different versions of various libraries than you have on another, so when a library is looking for a specific function, but you have a different version that does not include the function, it will fail.

If you're lucky, and the versions are close enough, then you'd be able to use the library on the other operating system as well. If not, then it won't work.

Issue B: Dependencies again. You'd also need to worry about the packages on the second operating system. If they are expecting a certain version of a library, then the library itself may be okay, but some of the software using it would not be. It's the same problem in reverse. Maybe a web server needs a library with a certain feature, but it's been replaced or renamed in the newer version you're installing. In this case, the web server will fail. This is always going to be a problem re-compiling an existing package with a binary distribution. It's easy to control what you're compiling, but hard to control all the other packages. And in this case, the library is very widely used, so it's quite likely to happen.

I'm not sure your intention here, but there are some options:

1. Compile a static library  
This adds all the required libraries into the library. It solves issue A, by ignoring libraries on your system, and bringing its own. Issue B would still be a problem though.

2. Compile the newer library on a virtual machine, then move it over. If you make sure you're using the same version of the operating system in the VM, you should be okay. Depending on the options you enable or disable at compile time, you could still run into issue A or B, but you can check the specification file in the source and make sure to compile it with the same options.

3. Compile on the host using a distributed compilation tool from another machine. If you're not wanting to compile on the host due to performance issues, this tool will let you offload the compiling to the other machine, while still using all the installed libraries on the host. This would give you the same caveats as the previous option.

4. Find an already made package with the version/feature you want, and install it. Problems A and B are both possible with this path, but at least there will be someone ahead of you who has tested it before, and possibly lists or provides information about how to make it work.
